HIGH TIDE
Pitch ↗Evidence index

Controller and transport results

High Tide starts with ENEC’s offshore warning. It routes arrivals sideways in the marine approach and verifies clearance beyond the intake approach. The original High Tide v1.0 model, local engine and run archive support the physical comparison.

How the controller routes a bloom

  • Choose a side. In the reversal run, cross-flow changes sign at 450 s. The controller switches from B to A after a 10 s delay and mirrors the angled plume line.
  • Choose sections. The model divides the line into six sections. For each approaching active track, it selects the track’s lateral band and its immediate neighbors when the track is within 13 m in x of the plume line. The active set is the union across tracks.
  • Step the transport. The solver advances positions in 0.25 s steps using along-flow, cross-flow, near-intake pull, deterministic dispersion and an intervention term. It turns off the active curtain when the outlet is declared closed or a power fault is triggered.
  • Check the outcome. Record intake entries, final outside positions, retained tracks and tracks that leave by another boundary. Record returns separately because a returned track can finish in more than one of those categories across runs. At a future test site, use measured current vectors and a surveyed clearance line to verify a route before switching on any sections.

What the matched runs reveal

Seed 42; 900 s; 900 arrivals per row. The first three configurations use the same reversal at 450 s. For controlled sections, the return-current case adds an inward flow at the outside boundary. These are physical transport runs.

Scenario Configuration Intake Outside at finish Retained Other Ever returned
Reversal No diversion 338 0 456 106 0
Reversal Fixed bubbles 0 33 722 145 360
Reversal Controlled sections 78 266 390 166 128
Reversal, 90 s switch delay Controlled sections 92 206 389 213 171
Reversal with return flow Controlled sections 78 71 585 166 331

Compared with no diversion, controlled sections had 260 fewer intake entries and 266 more outside at the finish. Fixed bubbles had the fewest intake entries in this reversal, with substantially more tracks retained. The longer switch delay and the return-flow case show what to instrument: time to change routes, and clearance after a track leaves the approach. The complete archive covers 11 scenarios, five configurations and three seeds.

What we will measure in the flume

Keep the same incoming distribution and flow for no diversion, fixed bubbles and controlled sections. Map water velocity with tracers, record the run from above, and report time to clearance, retention and returns through both outlets. Compare physical sections on measured air delivery, duty time and water velocity. Published field and flume experiments support including different airflow and wave conditions.

In a separate contained animal trial, use the same physical configuration with cues on and off. Report sustained water-relative motion, the change in exit fraction, recovery and non-target response. The flume comparison and the cue test produce different measurements; link them through exit fraction and return counts.
